doc.title: Peter Appleyard interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 4, 2012

title: Royal Air Force band service and the wing commander story
summary: Kept as a drummer in a military band, he refused the warrant officer's offer to sign on, and decades later shared a dressing room with the wing commander of the RAF bands.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: 1945. Yeah. And what was your job in the service?

Well once they found out I was a musician they sent me home to get my drums, which was great, because I wanted to see that lovely girl. And I had a weekend’s leave and brought it back. And it was a military band. And when it came time for me to be demobilized — I had to do 18 months — everyone, it was mandatory. Because we still were under the War Measures Act. We were having all that trouble with the Russians with Berlin, you remember the support we gave all the Berliners. The warrant officer, who was a real bad one, said to me, “Oh,” he said, “so Appleyard, you’re being demobilized.” I said, “Yes.” “Well,” he said, “if you’d like to sign on for five years” he

said, “I’ll make you a sergeant.” I said, “Oh I don’t think so.” He said, “There’s going to be another war and I can’t guarantee you’ll get back in the band.” I said, “I’ll take my chances.” So I’m leaving and he said, “Oh by the way, Appleyard, you’ll never make it in music.” So anyway about 15 years ago, the wing commander in charge of all the bands of the Royal Air Force, came over to Toronto to play a concert in the big band shell. And guess who was the other band? Me.

So anyway he was one of those stubby kind of guys, he was a wing commander, and he had to share my dressing room you see? “Oh,” he says, “Old chap, you were in the Air Force, were you?” I said, “Yes.” He said, “What rank were you?” I said, “I was a leading aircraftsman.” And I said, “I was attached to the number 1 radio-controlled fighter command band, eleven group.” “Oh Jolly Old Wheeler, good chap.” I said, “Yeah, when you see him tell him I’m still struggling to make it.”
“By the way, move that stuff off my dressing room table.”
